content: Polymer science is a specialized subfield of materials science that focuses on the study of polymers, particularly synthetic polymers such as plastics. This field encompasses researchers from various disciplines, including chemistry, physics, and engineering. Polymer science is divided into three primary sub-disciplines: 1. Polymer Chemistry (or Macromolecular Chemistry): This area is concerned with the chemical synthesis and chemical properties of polymers. 2. Polymer Physics: This sub-discipline focuses on the bulk properties of polymer materials and their engineering applications. 3. Polymer Characterization: This involves the analysis of the chemical structure and morphology of polymers, as well as the determination of their physical properties in relation to compositional and structural parameters. History of Polymer Science The origins of modern polymer science can be traced back to the 1830s with the work of Henri Braconnot. Braconnot, along with Christian Schönbein and others, developed derivatives of the natural polymer cellulose, leading to the creation of new semi-synthetic materials such as celluloid and cellulose acetate. The term polymer was first introduced in 1833 by Jöns Jakob Berzelius, although his contributions to polymer science in the modern sense were minimal. In the 1840s, Friedrich Ludersdorf and Nathaniel Hayward independently discovered that adding sulfur to raw natural rubber (polyisoprene) prevented the material from becoming sticky. This process, known as vulcanization, was patented by Charles Goodyear in the United States and by Thomas Hancock in the United Kingdom. Vulcanized rubber became the first commercially successful product of polymer research. In 1884, Hilaire de Chardonnet established the first artificial fiber plant, producing regenerated cellulose (viscose rayon) as a substitute for silk. However, this material was highly flammable. In 1907, Leo Baekeland invented Bakelite, the first synthetic polymer, which was a thermosetting phenol-formaldehyde resin. Despite advancements in polymer synthesis, the molecular nature of polymers was not fully understood until Hermann Staudinger's work in 1922. Staudinger proposed that polymers consist of long chains of atoms held together by covalent bonds, challenging the earlier association or aggregate theories proposed by Thomas Graham in 1861. Staudinger's groundbreaking work, which took over a decade to gain acceptance, earned him the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1953. The World War II era marked the rise of a robust commercial polymer industry. The limited availability of natural materials like silk and latex necessitated the production of synthetic substitutes such as rayon and neoprene. In subsequent years, the development of advanced polymers like Kevlar and Teflon further fueled the growth of the polymer industry. This industrial expansion was paralleled by the establishment of strong academic programs and research institutes. In 1946, Herman Mark founded the Polymer Research Institute at Brooklyn Polytechnic, the first U.S. research facility dedicated to polymer science. Mark also played a pioneering role in developing curricula and pedagogy for the field. In 1950, the POLY division of the American Chemical Society was formed, becoming the second-largest division within the organization with nearly 8,000 members. Nobel Prizes Related to Polymer Science 2005 (Chemistry): Robert Grubbs, Richard Schrock, and Yves Chauvin were awarded for their work on olefin metathesis. 2000 (Chemistry): Alan G. MacDiarmid, Alan J. Heeger, and Hideki Shirakawa were recognized for their contributions to electroactive polymers, which advanced molecular electronics. 1991 (Physics): Pierre-Gilles de Gennes received the prize for developing a generalized theory of phase transitions, with applications to ordering and phase transitions in polymers. 1974 (Chemistry): Paul J. Flory was honored for his contributions to theoretical polymer chemistry. 1963 (Chemistry): Giulio Natta and Karl Ziegler were awarded for their work in polymer synthesis, specifically Ziegler-Natta catalysis. 1953 (Chemistry): Hermann Staudinger was recognized for his contributions to the understanding of macromolecular chemistry.
